title: Won't look at it
stem:
You are an F2 doctor in general surgery. Ms Fry, 41, had an emergency operation for a perforated bowel five days ago and now has a stoma. She refuses to look at it, cries when the nurses change the bag, and says she "can't live like this".

She is otherwise recovering well and is due for discharge in a few days.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Tell her she must learn to manage the stoma before she can go home.
options.brief: Puts pressure on her rather than support.
options.detailed: Learning stoma care matters for discharge, but presenting it as a condition may increase her distress.

options.text: Ask the nurses to show her the stoma anyway, to help her get used to it.
options.detailed: Adjustment needs to happen at her pace, with support.

options.text: Ask her about how she is feeling and what worries her.
options.brief: Understanding her distress is the first step.
options.detailed: Her reaction is understandable after an emergency operation. Listening, and asking gently what she means by 'can't live like this', also helps you judge whether she is at risk.

options.text: Ask the stoma nurse specialist to see her.
options.brief: Specialist support for adjusting to a stoma.
options.detailed: Stoma nurses help patients come to terms with stomas and learn to manage them at their own pace.

options.text: Tell her about psychological and peer support for people with stomas.
options.brief: Talking to others in her situation can help.
options.detailed: Psychological support and contact with people who have adjusted to a stoma can make a big difference to body image and confidence.
She may need treatment for low mood, but this needs proper assessment first.

options.text: Reassure her that most people get used to their stoma.
options.detailed: Many people do adjust, but saying so now may make her feel her distress isn't being heard.

options.text: Arrange for the district nurses to manage her stoma at home.
options.brief: Avoids the issue rather than addressing it.
options.detailed: District nurses may support her at home, but this doesn't address her distress.

explanation.issue: This tests how you respond to a patient's distress about a change in body image after surgery.
explanation.keyDetails: She had an emergency stoma. She is distressed and can't look at it. She has said she 'can't live like this'. Discharge is near.
explanation.reasoning: [C] explores her feelings and any risk, [D] brings in specialist support, and [E] offers psychological and peer support. The distractors pressure her ([A], [B]), treat prematurely ([F]), dismiss her ([G]), or avoid the issue ([H]).
explanation.competing: [G] is well meant and often true, but she needs to feel heard before she can accept reassurance.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 2, responding to patients' emotional needs.
